# 42 Maxims: every maxim and quote

> 42 Maxims collects short rules for life that recur across religions, philosophies and periods. Every maxim lists exact quotes, each with its voice, work and locus (chapter, verse or page), translation, tradition, period and a verification label (verified, probable, disputed, unverified, misattributed). Maxims are ranked by Moral Rank, which measures how widely and independently traditions arrived at an idea (convergence, not truth or moral worth); ranks shift as sources are added.

When citing, link the maxim page and quote the wording exactly as shown there, with its source. Treat `probable` quotes as checked only against a secondary source, and do not attribute `unverified` or `misattributed` quotes to the people they are popularly credited to. The project's own writing and data are CC BY-SA 4.0; quotes remain the property of their authors and translators.

Maxims appear in Moral Rank order (The 42 first, then Emerging).

## Forgive, and keep forgiving.

https://42maxims.com/maxims/forgiveness/ · Moral Rank 100.0 · 8 traditions · The 42

Everyone stumbles, and everyone needs pardon at some point. Letting go of a grievance frees the one who forgives as much as the one forgiven.

- "Jesus saith unto him, I say not unto thee, Until seven times: but, Until seventy times seven." — Jesus, Matthew 18:22 (KJV), in answer to Peter asking how often he should forgive. Christianity; Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "Let them forgive and show indulgence. Yearn ye not that Allah may forgive you?" — The Qur'an, Qur'an 24:22 (Sura An-Nur), tr. Marmaduke Pickthall. Islam; Medieval (600 – 1500); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: Marmaduke Pickthall translation, as given on quran.com. Read it at: https://quran.com/24/22
- "The discretion of a man deferreth his anger; and it is his glory to pass over a transgression." — Book of Proverbs, Proverbs 19:11 (KJV). Judaism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "It is peculiar to man to love even those who do wrong." — Marcus Aurelius, Meditations, Book VII.22, tr. George Long. Stoicism; Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (George Long). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/15877
- "To err is human, to forgive, divine." — Alexander Pope, An Essay on Criticism (1711), Part II. English poetry & literature; Early modern (1500 – 1800); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: public domain. Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/7409
- "The one who loves forgives in this way: he forgives, he forgets, he blots out the sin, in love he turns toward the one he forgives." — Søren Kierkegaard, Works of Love (1847), tr. Howard V. and Edna H. Hong (Princeton University Press, 1995); checked in the Internet Archive scan of that edition (punctuation corrected to match it: colon after "in this way"). Existentialism / Absurdism; Modern (1800 – 1950); relation: similar; verified. Translation: tr. Howard V. and Edna H. Hong (copyright; short quotation). Read it at: https://archive.org/details/worksoflove0000kier
- "Forgiving trespasses is good always; / Forgetting them hath even higher praise;" — Tiruvalluvar, Tirukkural, kural 152, tr. G. U. Pope (1886); verse line break shown as /. Tamil ethics (Tirukkural); Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (G. U. Pope, W. H. Drew, J. Lazarus, F. W. Ellis). Read it at: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Tirukural/Chapter_16
- "He who forgives ends the quarrel." — Yoruba proverb, Yoruba proverb 24, as recorded and translated by A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-Speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (1894), ch. XIII. The saying is older than its 1894 recording.. Yoruba tradition; Modern (1800 – 1950); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (A. B. Ellis). Read it at: https://archive.sacred-texts.com/afr/yor/yor11.htm

## Tell the truth, or at least don't lie.

https://42maxims.com/maxims/tell-the-truth/ · Moral Rank 98.1 · 7 traditions · The 42

Honesty keeps our footing sure. Each small truth makes the world, and ourselves, a little easier to trust.

- "Tell the truth—or, at least, don't lie." — Jordan B. Peterson, 12 Rules for Life (2018), Rule 8 (rule title); Random House Canada edition, checked against the book's contents as shown on Google Books (that listing drops punctuation; dash corrected to the unspaced em dash of the printed chapter heading). Modern psychology & self-help; Contemporary (1950 – today); relation: expresses; verified. Read it at: https://books.google.com/books/about/12_Rules_for_Life.html?id=sxVHDwAAQBAJ
- "Lying lips are abomination to the LORD: but they that deal truly are his delight." — Book of Proverbs, Proverbs 12:22 (KJV). Judaism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "Wherefore putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour: for we are members one of another." — Paul the Apostle, Ephesians 4:25 (KJV). Christianity; Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "Speak the truth, do not yield to anger; give, if thou art asked for little; by these three steps thou wilt go near the gods." — The Buddha, Dhammapada 224, tr. F. Max Müller. Buddhism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Müller). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/2017
- "We are not called upon to step out onto the square and shout out the truth, to say out loud what we think—this is scary, we are not ready. But let us at least refuse to say what we do not think!" — Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn, Live Not by Lies (12 February 1974), tr. Yermolai Solzhenitsyn, as published by the Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn Center. Russian literature & thought; Contemporary (1950 – today); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: tr. Yermolai Solzhenitsyn (copyright; short quotation). Read it at: https://www.solzhenitsyncenter.org/live-not-by-lies
- "Above all, don’t lie to yourself. The man who lies to himself and listens to his own lie comes to such a pass that he cannot distinguish the truth within him, or around him, and so loses all respect for himself and for others." — Fyodor Dostoevsky, The Brothers Karamazov (1879–80), Book II, ch. 2 (Father Zossima), tr. Constance Garnett. Russian literature & thought; Modern (1800 – 1950); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Constance Garnett). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/28054
- "Say what is true! Do thy duty!" — Taittiriya Upanishad, Taittiriya Upanishad I.11.1, a teacher's parting charge to his pupil, tr. F. Max Müller (Sacred Books of the East 15, 1884). Hinduism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (F. Max Müller). Read it at: https://archive.sacred-texts.com/hin/sbe15/sbe15032.htm
- "One falsehood spoils a thousand truths." — Ashanti (Akan) proverb, Ashanti Proverbs, no. 609, tr. R. Sutherland Rattray (Oxford, 1916), from J. G. Christaller's Twi collection (1879). The saying is older than its recording.. Akan (Ashanti) tradition; Modern (1800 – 1950); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (R. S. Rattray). Read it at: https://archive.org/details/ashantiproverbst00rattuoft

## Treat others as you would wish to be treated.

https://42maxims.com/maxims/golden-rule/ · Moral Rank 96.8 · 9 traditions · The 42

Perhaps the most widely shared rule for living. Long before these traditions could read one another, each arrived at the same quiet test: before you act, put yourself in the other person's place.

- "What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others." — Confucius, Analects 15 (Wei Ling Gong), tr. James Legge. Confucianism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Legge). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/4094/pg4094.txt
- "That which is hateful to you do not do to another; that is the entire Torah, and the rest is its interpretation." — Hillel the Elder, Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 31a (William Davidson translation). Judaism; Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: Sefaria / William Davidson translation (CC BY-NC). Read it at: https://www.sefaria.org/Shabbat.31a
- "Therefore all things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them: for this is the law and the prophets." — Jesus, Matthew 7:12 (King James Version). Christianity; Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: KJV (public domain). Read it at: https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Matthew+7%3A12&version=KJV
- "And as ye would that men should do to you, do ye also to them likewise." — Jesus, Luke 6:31 (KJV). Christianity; Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Luke+6%3A31&version=KJV
- "Thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD." — Hebrew Bible (Torah), Leviticus 19:18 (KJV). Judaism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Leviticus+19%3A18&version=KJV
- "None of you will have faith till he wishes for his (Muslim) brother what he likes for himself." — The Prophet Muhammad (narrated by Anas), Sahih al-Bukhari 13. Islam; Medieval (600 – 1500); relation: similar; verified. Translation: Muhsin Khan translation, as given on sunnah.com. Read it at: https://sunnah.com/bukhari:13
- "Act only on that maxim whereby thou canst at the same time will that it should become a universal law." — Immanuel Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysic of Morals (1785), Second Section, tr. Thomas Kingsmill Abbott. Enlightenment thought; Early modern (1500 – 1800); relation: partial; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (T. K. Abbott). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/5682
- "So act as to treat humanity, whether in thine own person or in that of any other, in every case as an end withal, never as means only." — Immanuel Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysic of Morals (1785), Second Section, tr. Thomas Kingsmill Abbott. Enlightenment thought; Early modern (1500 – 1800); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (T. K. Abbott). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/5682
- "One should never do that to another which one regards as injurious to one's own self. This, in brief, is the rule of Righteousness." — Brihaspati (Mahabharata), Mahabharata, Anusasana Parva, Section CXIII (Brihaspati speaking to Yudhishthira), tr. Kisari Mohan Ganguli. Hinduism; Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Kisari Mohan Ganguli). Read it at: https://archive.sacred-texts.com/hin/m13/m13b078.htm
- "What his own soul has felt as bitter pain, / From making others feel should man abstain." — Tiruvalluvar, Tirukkural, kural 316, tr. G. U. Pope (1886); verse line break shown as /. Tamil ethics (Tirukkural); Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (G. U. Pope, W. H. Drew, J. Lazarus, F. W. Ellis). Read it at: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Tirukural/Chapter_32
- "It is to regard the state of others as one's own, the houses of others as one's own, the persons of others as one's self." — Mozi, Mozi, Book 4, Universal Love II, tr. W. P. Mei (1929). Wording checked via the page text shown in a web search index; the page itself blocks automated fetching, so not checked directly.. Mohism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; probable. Translation: translation (W. P. Mei), as published on ctext.org. Read it at: https://ctext.org/mozi/universal-love-ii
- "He ought to pity the malignant tendencies of others; to rejoice over their excellences; to help them in their straits; to rescue them from their perils; to regard their gains as if they were his own, and their losses in the same way" — Treatise of the Most Exalted One on Action and Response, The Thai-Shang Tractate of Actions and Their Retributions (Taishang Ganying Pian), 3, tr. James Legge (Sacred Books of the East 40, 1891). Taoism; Medieval (600 – 1500); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (James Legge). Read it at: https://archive.sacred-texts.com/tao/sbe40/sbe4018.htm

## Speak kindly, or keep silent.

https://42maxims.com/maxims/guard-your-tongue/ · Moral Rank 94.3 · 8 traditions · The 42

Words can heal or wound, and once spoken they cannot be taken back. A little restraint in speech spares others pain and spares us a good deal of trouble.

- "anybody who believes in Allah and the Last Day should talk what is good or keep quiet." — The Prophet Muhammad (narrated by Abu Huraira), Sahih al-Bukhari 6018. Islam; Medieval (600 – 1500); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: Muhsin Khan translation, as given on sunnah.com. Read it at: https://sunnah.com/bukhari:6018
- "Whoso keepeth his mouth and his tongue keepeth his soul from troubles." — Book of Proverbs, Proverbs 21:23 (KJV). Judaism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "Death and life are in the power of the tongue: and they that love it shall eat the fruit thereof." — Book of Proverbs, Proverbs 18:21 (KJV). Judaism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "Do not speak harshly to anybody; those who are spoken to will answer thee in the same way. Angry speech is painful, blows for blows will touch thee." — The Buddha, Dhammapada 133, tr. F. Max Müller. Buddhism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Müller). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/2017
- "Even so the tongue is a little member, and boasteth great things. Behold, how great a matter a little fire kindleth! And the tongue is a fire, a world of iniquity: so is the tongue among our members, that it defileth the whole body, and setteth on fire the course of nature; and it is set on fire of hell." — James, James 3:5–6 (KJV). Christianity; Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "Be mostly silent, or speak merely what is needful, and in few words." — Epictetus, Enchiridion XXXIII, tr. Thomas Wentworth Higginson. Stoicism; Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Higginson). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/45109
- "Silence is more profitable unto thee than abundance of speech." — Ptahhotep, The Instruction of Ptah-hotep, §24, tr. Battiscombe G. Gunn (1906). Ancient Egyptian wisdom literature; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Battiscombe G. Gunn). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/30508
- "“Guard your tongue in youth,” said the old chief, Wabashaw, “and in age you may mature a thought that will be of service to your people!”" — Ohiyesa (Charles A. Eastman), The Soul of the Indian (1911), ch. IV (Barbarism and the Moral Code) (Wabasha, a Dakota chief, quoted by Eastman). Dakota (Sioux) tradition; Modern (1800 – 1950); relation: similar; verified. Translation: written in English by the author. Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/340
- "When pleasant words are easy, bitter words to use, / Is, leaving sweet ripe fruit, the sour unripe to choose." — Tiruvalluvar, Tirukkural, kural 100, tr. G. U. Pope (1886); verse line break shown as /. Tamil ethics (Tirukkural); Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (G. U. Pope, W. H. Drew, J. Lazarus, F. W. Ellis). Read it at: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Tirukural/Chapter_10
- "In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin: but he that refraineth his lips is wise." — Book of Proverbs, Proverbs 10:19 (KJV). Judaism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10

## Be slow to anger; master yourself.

https://42maxims.com/maxims/master-your-anger/ · Moral Rank 94.0 · 8 traditions · The 42

Anger arrives quickly and leaves damage behind it. Real strength, these voices agree, lies less in overpowering others than in holding the reins of our own temper.

- "He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city." — Book of Proverbs, Proverbs 16:32 (KJV). Judaism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath:" — James, James 1:19 (KJV). Christianity; Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "He who holds back rising anger like a rolling chariot, him I call a real driver; other people are but holding the reins." — The Buddha, Dhammapada 222, tr. F. Max Müller. Buddhism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Müller). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/2017
- "The strong is not the one who overcomes the people by his strength, but the strong is the one who controls himself while in anger." — The Prophet Muhammad (narrated by Abu Huraira), Sahih al-Bukhari 6114. Islam; Medieval (600 – 1500); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: Muhsin Khan translation, as given on sunnah.com. Read it at: https://sunnah.com/bukhari:6114
- "Who give alms, alike in prosperity and in success, and who master their anger, and forgive others! God loveth the doers of good." — The Qur'an, Qur'an 3:134 (Sura Al 'Imran), tr. J. M. Rodwell. Islam; Medieval (600 – 1500); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (J. M. Rodwell). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/2800
- "Be not silent, but beware of interruption and of answering words with heat. Put it far from thee; control thyself. The wrathful heart speaketh fiery words; it darteth out at the man of peace that approacheth, stopping his path." — Ptahhotep, The Instruction of Ptah-hotep, §25, tr. Battiscombe G. Gunn (1906). Ancient Egyptian wisdom literature; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Battiscombe G. Gunn). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/30508
- "Though a man should conquer thousands and thousands of valiant (foes), greater will be his victory if he conquers nobody but himself." — Mahavira (Uttaradhyayana Sutra), Uttaradhyayana Sutra IX.34, tr. Hermann Jacobi (Sacred Books of the East 45, 1895). Self-conquest in general rather than anger alone.. Jainism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Hermann Jacobi). Read it at: https://archive.sacred-texts.com/jai/sbe45/sbe4511.htm
- "Anger does nobody good, / But patience is the father of kindness. / Anger draws arrows from the quiver, / But good words draw kola-nuts from the bag." — Yoruba proverb, Yoruba aphorism 5 (couplet sayings), as recorded and translated by A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-Speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (1894), ch. XIII; line breaks shown as /. The saying is older than its 1894 recording.. Yoruba tradition; Modern (1800 – 1950); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (A. B. Ellis). Read it at: https://archive.sacred-texts.com/afr/yor/yor11.htm
- "Let us cease from wrath, and refrain from angry looks. Nor let us be resentful when others differ from us. For all men have hearts, and each heart has its own leanings." — Prince Shōtoku, Seventeen-Article Constitution (604), art. X, in Nihongi, Book XXII, tr. W. G. Aston (1896). Early Japanese thought (Shōtoku); Medieval (600 – 1500); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (W. G. Aston). Read it at: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Nihongi/Book_XXII

## Be merciful to every living being.

https://42maxims.com/maxims/be-merciful/ · Moral Rank 91.8 · 7 traditions · The 42

Mercy is kindness offered where it was not earned. Traditions across the world ask us to widen our care, from family to stranger to every creature that breathes, and find that a softer heart is also a freer one.

- "Even as a mother protects with her life Her child, her only child, So with a boundless heart Should one cherish all living beings;" — The Buddha, Karaniya Metta Sutta (Sn 1.8), tr. the Amaravati Sangha. Buddhism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: Amaravati Sangha (free distribution). Read it at: https://www.accesstoinsight.org/tipitaka/kn/snp/snp.1.08.amar.html
- "Be ye therefore merciful, as your Father also is merciful." — Jesus, Luke 6:36 (KJV). Christianity; Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "Allah will not be merciful to those who are not merciful to mankind." — The Prophet Muhammad (narrated by Jarir bin Abdullah), Sahih al-Bukhari 7376. Islam; Medieval (600 – 1500); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: Muhsin Khan translation, as given on sunnah.com. Read it at: https://sunnah.com/bukhari:7376
- "The merciful are shown mercy by Ar-Rahman. Be merciful on the earth, and you will be shown mercy from Who is above the heavens." — The Prophet Muhammad (narrated by Abdullah bin 'Amr), Jami` at-Tirmidhi 1924 (graded hasan sahih by at-Tirmidhi). Islam; Medieval (600 – 1500); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: English translation as given on sunnah.com. Read it at: https://sunnah.com/tirmidhi:1924
- "The quality of mercy is not strain’d, It droppeth as the gentle rain from heaven Upon the place beneath. It is twice blest, It blesseth him that gives and him that takes." — William Shakespeare (spoken by Portia), The Merchant of Venice, Act 4, Scene 1 (Portia's speech); line breaks removed. English poetry & literature; Early modern (1500 – 1800); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public domain. Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/1515
- "The divine voice of thunder repeats the same, Da Da Da, that is, Be subdued, Give, Be merciful. Therefore let that triad be taught, Subduing, Giving, and Mercy." — Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, Brihadaranyaka Upanishad V.2.3, tr. F. Max Müller (Sacred Books of the East 15, 1884). Hinduism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (F. Max Müller). Read it at: https://archive.sacred-texts.com/hin/sbe15/sbe15080.htm
- "The sons of Adam are members one of another, for in their creation they have a common origin. If the vicissitudes of fortune involve one member in pain, all the other members will feel a sympathy. Thou, who art indifferent to other men's affliction, if they call thee a man art unworthy of the name." — Saadi, Gulistan, ch. I, story X, tr. James Ross (1823), in Persian Literature, vol. 2 (Colonial Press, 1900); verse rendered as prose by the translator. Persian poetry & literature; Medieval (600 – 1500); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (James Ross). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/13060
- "Not to aid one in distress is to kill him in your heart." — Yoruba proverb, Yoruba proverb 71, as recorded and translated by A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-Speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (1894), ch. XIII. The saying is older than its 1894 recording.. Yoruba tradition; Modern (1800 – 1950); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (A. B. Ellis). Read it at: https://archive.sacred-texts.com/afr/yor/yor11.htm

## Give freely; generosity enriches the giver.

https://42maxims.com/maxims/generosity/ · Moral Rank 87.6 · 7 traditions · The 42

What we give away has a strange way of coming back as a fuller life. An open hand makes room for connection, and it loosens the grip that possessions can have on us.

- "remember the words of the Lord Jesus, how he said, It is more blessed to give than to receive." — Paul the Apostle (quoting Jesus), Acts 20:35 (KJV). Christianity; Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "The liberal soul shall be made fat: and he that watereth shall be watered also himself." — Book of Proverbs, Proverbs 11:25 (KJV). Judaism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "The more that he expends for others, the more does he possess of his own; the more that he gives to others, the more does he have himself." — Laozi, Tao Te Ching, ch. 81, tr. James Legge. Taoism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Legge). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/216
- "Charity does not decrease wealth," — The Prophet Muhammad (narrated by Abu Huraira), Sahih Muslim 2588. Islam; Medieval (600 – 1500); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: Abdul Hamid Siddiqui translation, as given on sunnah.com. Read it at: https://sunnah.com/muslim:2588
- "fools only do not praise liberality; a wise man rejoices in liberality," — The Buddha, Dhammapada 177, tr. F. Max Müller. Buddhism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Müller). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/2017
- "That which goeth into the storehouse must come out therefrom; and bread is to be shared. He that is grasping in entertainment shall himself have an empty belly" — Ptahhotep, The Instruction of Ptah-hotep, §34, tr. Battiscombe G. Gunn (1906). Ancient Egyptian wisdom literature; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Battiscombe G. Gunn). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/30508
- "Therefore the child must early learn the beauty of generosity. He is taught to give what he prizes most, and that he may taste the happiness of giving, he is made at an early age the family almoner." — Ohiyesa (Charles A. Eastman), The Soul of the Indian (1911), ch. IV (Barbarism and the Moral Code). Dakota (Sioux) tradition; Modern (1800 – 1950); relation: similar; verified. Translation: written in English by the author. Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/340

## Meet hatred with love and evil with good.

https://42maxims.com/maxims/overcome-hatred-with-love/ · Moral Rank 86.8 · 6 traditions · The 42

Answering harm with harm only keeps the wheel turning. Many traditions ask something harder and braver: to break the cycle by returning kindness, even to an enemy.

- "For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love, this is an old rule." — The Buddha, Dhammapada 5, tr. F. Max Müller. Buddhism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Müller). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/2017
- "But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you;" — Jesus, Matthew 5:44 (KJV). Christianity; Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "If thine enemy be hungry, give him bread to eat; and if he be thirsty, give him water to drink:" — Book of Proverbs, Proverbs 25:21 (KJV). Judaism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "Turn away evil by what is better, and lo! he between whom and thyself was enmity, shall be as though he were a warm friend." — The Qur'an, Qur'an 41:34 (Sura Fussilat, 'The Made Plain'), tr. J. M. Rodwell. Islam; Medieval (600 – 1500); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (J. M. Rodwell). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/2800
- "Let a man overcome anger by love, let him overcome evil by good; let him overcome the greedy by liberality, the liar by truth!" — The Buddha, Dhammapada 223, tr. F. Max Müller. Buddhism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Müller). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/2017
- "Hatred is increased by being reciprocated, and can on the other hand be destroyed by love." — Baruch Spinoza, Ethics (1677), Part III, Prop. XLIII, tr. R. H. M. Elwes. Rationalism; Early modern (1500 – 1800); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (R. H. M. Elwes). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/3800
- "To punish wrong, with kindly benefits the doers ply; / Thus shame their souls; but pass the ill unheeded by." — Tiruvalluvar, Tirukkural, kural 314, tr. G. U. Pope (1886); verse line break shown as /. Tamil ethics (Tirukkural); Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (G. U. Pope, W. H. Drew, J. Lazarus, F. W. Ellis). Read it at: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Tirukural/Chapter_32

## Do what is right, even when you are afraid.

https://42maxims.com/maxims/courage/ · Moral Rank 86.4 · 7 traditions · The 42

Courage is not the absence of fear but the choice to act well in its presence. Most of the good we do asks a little bravery of us.

- "Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest." — Book of Joshua, Joshua 1:9 (KJV). Judaism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "To see what is right and not to do it is want of courage." — Confucius, Analects 2.24, tr. James Legge. Confucianism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Legge). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/4094
- "the Brave man chooses his line and withstands danger either because to do so is honourable, or because not to do so is base." — Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book III, tr. D. P. Chase. Greek philosophy; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Chase). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/8438
- "For God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind." — Paul the Apostle, 2 Timothy 1:7 (KJV). Christianity; Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "The very cave you are afraid to enter turns out to be the source of what you are looking for." — Joseph Campbell, A Joseph Campbell Companion (1991), ed. Diane K. Osbon, 'In the Field', from her notes of his talk; checked in the Internet Archive scan of the HarperCollins 1991 edition. The popular form "The cave you fear to enter holds the treasure you seek" is not found in his works; Quote Investigator's earliest print instance is 2004. Comparative mythology; Contemporary (1950 – today); relation: partial; verified. Read it at: https://archive.org/details/josephcampbellco0000camp
- "vulnerability is not weakness. … vulnerability is our most accurate measurement of courage." — Brené Brown, Interview on NPR's TED Radio Hour, “Can We Gain Strength From Shame?”, 11 March 2013 (NPR transcript). Modern psychology & self-help; Contemporary (1950 – today); relation: similar; verified. Read it at: https://www.npr.org/transcripts/174033560
- "What we fear doing most is usually what we most need to do." — Tim Ferriss, “Fear-Setting”, tim.blog (2017), adapted from The 4-Hour Workweek and Tools of Titans. Modern psychology & self-help; Contemporary (1950 – today); relation: similar; verified. Read it at: https://tim.blog/2017/05/15/fear-setting/
- "“Let neither cold, hunger, nor pain, nor the fear of them, neither the bristling teeth of danger nor the very jaws of death itself, prevent you from doing a good deed,” said an old chief to a scout" — Ohiyesa (Charles A. Eastman), The Soul of the Indian (1911), ch. IV (Barbarism and the Moral Code) (an unnamed chief, quoted by Eastman). Dakota (Sioux) tradition; Modern (1800 – 1950); relation: similar; verified. Translation: written in English by the author. Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/340

## Seek counsel: don't decide big things alone.

https://42maxims.com/maxims/seek-counsel/ · Moral Rank 84.8 · 8 traditions · The 42

No one sees every side of a hard question. Before a weighty decision, it is wise to ask people who know more, or who will tell us plainly where we are wrong, and to listen to what they say.

- "Without counsel purposes are disappointed: but in the multitude of counsellors they are established." — Book of Proverbs, Proverbs 15:22 (KJV). Judaism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety." — Book of Proverbs, Proverbs 11:14 (KJV). Judaism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "The way of a fool is right in his own eyes: but he that hearkeneth unto counsel is wise." — Book of Proverbs, Proverbs 12:15 (KJV). Judaism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "And who hearken to their Lord, and observe prayer, and whose affairs are guided by mutual COUNSEL, and who give alms of that with which we have enriched them;" — The Qur'an, Qur'an 42:38 (Sura Ash-Shura, 'Counsel'), tr. J. M. Rodwell; the capitals are Rodwell's. Islam; Medieval (600 – 1500); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (J. M. Rodwell). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/2800
- "When you have doubts about any great matter, consult with your own mind; consult with your high ministers and officers; consult with the common people; consult the tortoise-shell and divining stalks." — The count of Khî (Jizi), in the Book of Documents, Shu King (Book of Documents), The Great Plan, tr. James Legge (Sacred Books of the East 3, 1879); the advice includes divination. Confucianism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (James Legge). Read it at: https://archive.sacred-texts.com/cfu/sbe03/sbe03031.htm
- "Do not listen to unsubstantiated words; do not follow plans about which you have not sought counsel." — Emperor Shun (to Yü), in the Book of Documents, Shu King (Book of Documents), The Counsels of the Great Yü, tr. James Legge (Sacred Books of the East 3, 1879); an 'Old Text' chapter, which most scholars judge a 3rd–4th-century CE reconstruction. Confucianism; Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (James Legge). Read it at: https://archive.sacred-texts.com/cfu/sbe03/sbe03010.htm
- "That man is altogether best who considers all things himself and marks what will be better afterwards and at the end; and he, again, is good who listens to a good adviser; but whoever neither thinks for himself nor keeps in mind what another tells him, he is an unprofitable man." — Hesiod, Works and Days, ll. 293–297, tr. Hugh G. Evelyn-White (1914). Ancient Greek epic & drama; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (H. G. Evelyn-White). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/348
- "When a king has good councillors, then his reign is peaceful." — Ashanti (Akan) proverb, Ashanti Proverbs, no. 416, tr. R. Sutherland Rattray (Oxford, 1916), p. 115, from J. G. Christaller's Twi collection (1879); wording checked against the page scan. The saying is older than its recording.. Akan (Ashanti) tradition; Modern (1800 – 1950); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (R. S. Rattray). Read it at: https://archive.org/details/ashantiproverbst00rattuoft/page/n120/mode/1up
- "If you see an intelligent man who tells you where true treasures are to be found, who shows what is to be avoided, and administers reproofs, follow that wise man; it will be better, not worse, for those who follow him." — The Buddha, Dhammapada 76, tr. F. Max Müller. Buddhism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Müller). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/2017
- "What power can work his fall, who faithful ministers / Employs, that thunder out reproaches when he errs." — Tiruvalluvar, Tirukkural, kural 447, tr. G. U. Pope (1886); verse line break shown as /. Tamil ethics (Tirukkural); Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (G. U. Pope, W. H. Drew, J. Lazarus, F. W. Ellis). Read it at: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Tirukural/Chapter_45
- "Decisions on important matters should not be made by one person alone. They should be discussed with many." — Prince Shōtoku, Seventeen-Article Constitution (604), art. XVII, in Nihongi, Book XXII, tr. W. G. Aston (1896); footnote marker removed. Early Japanese thought (Shōtoku); Medieval (600 – 1500); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (W. G. Aston). Read it at: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Nihongi/Book_XXII

## Look to your own faults before judging others.

https://42maxims.com/maxims/examine-yourself-first/ · Moral Rank 84.6 · 6 traditions · The 42

It is easy to see what others get wrong and hard to see our own failings. Turning the light on ourselves first makes us both wiser and kinder.

- "And why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother's eye, but considerest not the beam that is in thine own eye?" — Jesus, Matthew 7:3 (KJV). Christianity; Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "Not the perversities of others, not their sins of commission or omission, but his own misdeeds and negligences should a sage take notice of." — The Buddha, Dhammapada 50, tr. F. Max Müller. Buddhism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Müller). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/2017
- "The fault of others is easily perceived, but that of oneself is difficult to perceive;" — The Buddha, Dhammapada 252, tr. F. Max Müller. Buddhism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Müller). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/2017
- "He who requires much from himself and little from others, will keep himself from being the object of resentment." — Confucius, Analects 15.14, tr. James Legge. Confucianism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Legge). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/4094
- "It is the action of an uninstructed person to reproach others for his own misfortunes; of one entering upon instruction, to reproach himself; and one perfectly instructed, to reproach neither others nor himself." — Epictetus, Enchiridion V, tr. Thomas Wentworth Higginson. Stoicism; Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Higginson). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/45109
- "If only there were evil people somewhere insidiously committing evil deeds, and it were necessary only to separate them from the rest of us and destroy them. But the line dividing good and evil cuts through the heart of every human being." — Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn, The Gulag Archipelago, vol. 1 (1973), tr. Thomas P. Whitney (Harper & Row, 1974, Parts I–II); checked in the Internet Archive scan of that edition. Russian literature & thought; Contemporary (1950 – today); relation: similar; verified. Translation: tr. Thomas P. Whitney (copyright; short quotation). Read it at: https://archive.org/details/gulagarchipelago1974solz
- "How couldst thou forget thine own faults and busy thyself with the faults of others? Whoso doeth this is accursed of Me." — Bahá’u’lláh, The Hidden Words, Arabic no. 26, tr. Shoghi Effendi. Bahá’í Faith; Modern (1800 – 1950); relation: similar; verified. Translation: authorised translation (Shoghi Effendi). Read it at: https://www.bahai.org/library/authoritative-texts/bahaullah/hidden-words/2

## Welcome the stranger.

https://42maxims.com/maxims/welcome-the-stranger/ · Moral Rank 81.3 · 6 traditions · The 42

Almost every tradition treats the guest and the traveller as someone to honour. Opening our door, and our table, reminds us that we too have been strangers somewhere.

- "But the stranger that dwelleth with you shall be unto you as one born among you, and thou shalt love him as thyself; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt:" — Hebrew Bible (Torah), Leviticus 19:34 (KJV). Judaism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares." — Epistle to the Hebrews, Hebrews 13:2 (KJV). Christianity; Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "anybody who believes in Allah and the Last Day should entertain his guest generously" — The Prophet Muhammad (narrated by Abu Huraira), Sahih al-Bukhari 6018. Islam; Medieval (600 – 1500); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: Muhsin Khan translation, as given on sunnah.com. Read it at: https://sunnah.com/bukhari:6018
- "Stranger, though a still poorer man should come here, it would not be right for me to insult him, for all strangers and beggars are from Jove." — Homer (Eumaeus the swineherd), Odyssey, Book XIV, tr. Samuel Butler. Ancient Greek epic & drama; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Samuel Butler). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/1727
- "The hospitality of the wigwam is only limited by the institution of war. Yet, if an enemy should honor us with a call, his trust will not be misplaced, and he will go away convinced that he has met with a royal host! Our honor is the guarantee for his safety, so long as he is within the camp." — Ohiyesa (Charles A. Eastman), The Soul of the Indian (1911), ch. II (The Family Altar). Dakota (Sioux) tradition; Modern (1800 – 1950); relation: similar; verified. Translation: written in English by the author. Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/340
- "Let thy guest be to thee like unto a god!" — Taittiriya Upanishad, Taittiriya Upanishad I.11.2, tr. F. Max Müller (Sacred Books of the East 15, 1884). Hinduism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (F. Max Müller). Read it at: https://archive.sacred-texts.com/hin/sbe15/sbe15032.htm

## Give thanks.

https://42maxims.com/maxims/gratitude/ · Moral Rank 76.9 · 7 traditions · The 42

Gratitude turns what we have into enough, and it notices the kindness we would otherwise take for granted. Saying thank you, to people and to life, softens the heart and makes room for joy.

- "And when your Lord proclaimed: If ye give thanks, I will give you more;" — The Qur'an, Qur'an 14:7 (Sura Ibrahim), tr. Marmaduke Pickthall. Islam; Medieval (600 – 1500); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: Marmaduke Pickthall translation, as given on quran.com. Read it at: https://quran.com/14/7
- "In every thing give thanks: for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you." — Paul the Apostle, 1 Thessalonians 5:18 (KJV). Christianity; Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "O give thanks unto the LORD; for he is good: because his mercy endureth for ever." — Psalms, Psalm 118:1 (KJV). Judaism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "He who does not thank the people is not thankful to Allah." — The Prophet Muhammad (narrated by Abu Hurayrah), Sunan Abi Dawud 4811. Islam; Medieval (600 – 1500); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: Ahmad Hasan translation, as given on sunnah.com. Read it at: https://sunnah.com/abudawud:4811
- "Respect, humility, contentment, gratitude, hearing the Dhamma on timely occasions: This is the highest protection." — The Buddha, Maha-mangala Sutta (Sn 2.4), tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu. Buddhism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: Thanissaro Bhikkhu (free distribution). Read it at: https://www.accesstoinsight.org/tipitaka/kn/snp/snp.2.04.than.html
- "we should sometimes try to look upon our possessions in the light in which they would appear if we had lost them" — Arthur Schopenhauer, Counsels and Maxims (from Parerga and Paralipomena, 1851), ch. II, §14, tr. T. Bailey Saunders. 19th-century German philosophy; Modern (1800 – 1950); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (T. Bailey Saunders). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10715
- "a gratitude practice is a very, very potent way in which you can steer your mental and physical health in positive directions" — Andrew Huberman, Huberman Lab, “The Science of Gratitude & How to Build a Gratitude Practice” (22 Nov 2021), spoken at 12:08 of the full episode (in the “Introduction” section of the episode); wording matches both the official transcript (re-checked Oct 2026) and the recording’s captions. Modern psychology & self-help; Contemporary (1950 – today); relation: partial; verified. Read it at: https://www.hubermanlab.com/episode/the-science-of-gratitude-and-how-to-build-a-gratitude-practice
- "'Tis never good to let the thought of good things done thee pass away; / Of things not good, 'tis good to rid thy memory that very day." — Tiruvalluvar, Tirukkural, kural 108, tr. G. U. Pope (1886); verse line break shown as /. Tamil ethics (Tirukkural); Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (G. U. Pope, W. H. Drew, J. Lazarus, F. W. Ellis). Read it at: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Tirukural/Chapter_11

## Remember that you will die, and live well today.

https://42maxims.com/maxims/remember-death/ · Moral Rank 74.6 · 5 traditions · The 42

Our days are numbered, and remembering it is not morbid but clarifying. Keeping death in view shrinks petty quarrels and turns us back towards what is good while we still can.

- "Do not act as if thou wert going to live ten thousand years. Death hangs over thee. While thou livest, while it is in thy power, be good." — Marcus Aurelius, Meditations, Book IV.17, tr. George Long. Stoicism; Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (George Long). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/15877
- "So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom." — Psalms (attributed to Moses), Psalm 90:12 (KJV). Judaism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "The world does not know that we must all come to an end here;--but those who know it, their quarrels cease at once." — The Buddha, Dhammapada 6, tr. F. Max Müller. Buddhism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Müller). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/2017
- "Where death waits for us is uncertain; let us look for him everywhere. The premeditation of death is the premeditation of liberty; he who has learned to die has unlearned to serve." — Michel de Montaigne, Essays, Book I, ch. 19, “That to study philosophy is to learn to die”, tr. Charles Cotton, ed. W. C. Hazlitt. Renaissance humanism; Early modern (1500 – 1800); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Charles Cotton). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/3600
- "As a dew-drop dangling on the top of a blade of Kusa-grass lasts but a short time, even so the life of men; Gautama, be careful all the while!" — Mahavira (Uttaradhyayana Sutra), Uttaradhyayana Sutra X.2, tr. Hermann Jacobi (Sacred Books of the East 45, 1895). Jainism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Hermann Jacobi). Read it at: https://archive.sacred-texts.com/jai/sbe45/sbe4512.htm

## Make time for stillness.

https://42maxims.com/maxims/be-still/ · Moral Rank 73.4 · 6 traditions · The 42

Much of our restlessness comes from never stopping. Contemplatives, philosophers and psalmists alike point to a quiet place within, always available, where we can rest, see clearly and return refreshed.

- "The (state of) vacancy should be brought to the utmost degree, and that of stillness guarded with unwearying vigour." — Laozi, Tao Te Ching, ch. 16, tr. James Legge. Taoism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Legge). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/216
- "it is in thy power whenever thou shalt choose to retire into thyself. For nowhere either with more quiet or more freedom from trouble does a man retire than into his own soul," — Marcus Aurelius, Meditations, Book IV.3, tr. George Long. Stoicism; Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (George Long). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/15877
- "I have discovered that all the unhappiness of men arises from one single fact, that they cannot stay quietly in their own chamber." — Blaise Pascal, Pensées, no. 139, tr. W. F. Trotter. Christianity; Early modern (1500 – 1800); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (W. F. Trotter). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/18269
- "Be still, and know that I am God:" — Psalms, Psalm 46:10 (KJV); stillness here is in the presence of God. Judaism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: partial; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "we must reserve a backshop, wholly our own and entirely free, wherein to settle our true liberty, our principal solitude and retreat." — Michel de Montaigne, Essays, Book I, ch. 38, “Of solitude”, tr. Charles Cotton, ed. W. C. Hazlitt. Renaissance humanism; Early modern (1500 – 1800); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Charles Cotton). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/3600
- "If you ask: “What are the fruits of silence?” he will say: “They are self-control, true courage or endurance, patience, dignity, and reverence. Silence is the cornerstone of character.”" — Ohiyesa (Charles A. Eastman), The Soul of the Indian (1911), ch. IV (Barbarism and the Moral Code). Dakota (Sioux) tradition; Modern (1800 – 1950); relation: similar; verified. Translation: written in English by the author. Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/340
- "Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God. And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus." — Paul the Apostle, Philippians 4:6–7 (KJV); "be careful for nothing" means "do not be anxious"; the peace comes through prayer rather than stillness as such. Christianity; Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: partial; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10

## Don't speak ill of people behind their backs.

https://42maxims.com/maxims/dont-backbite/ · Moral Rank 72.7 · 7 traditions · The 42

Talk about someone who is not there to answer can quietly wound them and divide friends. Many traditions single out backbiting and talebearing as a wrong of their own: what we would not say to a person's face, or what was told us in confidence, is better left unsaid.

- "neither let the one of you traduce another in his absence. Would any one of you like to eat the flesh of his dead brother? Surely ye would loathe it." — Qur'an, Qur'an 49:12 (Sura Al-Hujurat, 'The Apartments'), tr. J. M. Rodwell. Islam; Medieval (600 – 1500); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (J. M. Rodwell). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/2800
- "Woe to every BACKBITER, Defamer!" — Qur'an, Qur'an 104:1 (Sura Al-Humaza, 'The Backbiter'), tr. J. M. Rodwell; capitals as printed (Rodwell capitalises the word that names the sura). Islam; Medieval (600 – 1500); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (J. M. Rodwell). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/2800
- "Thou shalt not go up and down as a talebearer among thy people" — Authors of the Torah, Leviticus 19:16 (KJV), first clause. Judaism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "A froward man soweth strife: and a whisperer separateth chief friends." — Book of Proverbs, Proverbs 16:28 (KJV). Judaism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "Abandoning divisive speech he abstains from divisive speech. What he has heard here he does not tell there to break those people apart from these people here. What he has heard there he does not tell here to break these people apart from those people there." — The Buddha, Cunda Kammaraputta Sutta (AN 10.176), tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu; divisive speech is listed apart from abusive speech. Buddhism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: Thanissaro Bhikkhu (free distribution). Read it at: https://www.accesstoinsight.org/tipitaka/an/an10/an10.176.than.html
- "To tell, as we go along, what we have heard on the way, is to cast away our virtue." — Confucius, Analects 17.14 (Yang Huo), tr. James Legge. Confucianism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Legge). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/4094
- "and especially not on men, so as either to blame, or praise, or make comparisons." — Epictetus, Enchiridion XXXIII, tr. Thomas Wentworth Higginson; on topics of conversation, so it covers praise and comparison as well as blame. Stoicism; Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: partial; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Higginson). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/45109
- "In presence though unkindly words you speak, say not / In absence words whose ill result exceeds your thought." — Tiruvalluvar, Tirukkural, kural 184 (ch. 19, 'Not backbiting'), tr. G. U. Pope (1886); verse line break shown as ' / '. Tamil ethics (Tirukkural); Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (G. U. Pope, W. H. Drew, J. Lazarus, F. W. Ellis). Read it at: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Tirukural/Chapter_19
- "Beware of making enmity by thy words, setting one noble against the other by perverting truth. Overstep it not, neither repeat that which any man, be he prince or peasant, saith in opening the heart; it is abhorrent to the soul." — Ptahhotep, The Instruction of Ptah-hotep, §8, tr. Battiscombe G. Gunn (1906). Ancient Egyptian wisdom literature; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Battiscombe G. Gunn). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/30508

## Defend the widow, the orphan and the poor.

https://42maxims.com/maxims/defend-the-vulnerable/ · Moral Rank 72.0 · 6 traditions · The 42

Those without a protector are the easiest to overlook and to wrong. From the law codes of Babylon and the instructions of Egyptian kings to the Hebrew prophets, the Qur'an and Mencius, the measure of a just person or ruler is how they treat the widow, the fatherless and the needy, and whether they speak up for them.

- "Open thy mouth for the dumb in the cause of all such as are appointed to destruction. Open thy mouth, judge righteously, and plead the cause of the poor and needy." — Book of Proverbs, Proverbs 31:8–9 (KJV). Judaism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "And oppress not the widow, nor the fatherless, the stranger, nor the poor; and let none of you imagine evil against his brother in your heart." — Zechariah, Zechariah 7:10 (KJV). Judaism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "Ye shall not afflict any widow, or fatherless child." — Authors of the Torah, Exodus 22:22 (KJV). Judaism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "Defend the poor and fatherless: do justice to the afflicted and needy." — The Psalmists, Psalm 82:3 (KJV). Judaism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world." — James, James 1:27 (KJV). Christianity; Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "As to the orphan therefore wrong him not; And as to him that asketh of thee, chide him not away;" — Qur'an, Qur'an 93:9–10 (Sura Ad-Duha, 'The Brightness'), tr. J. M. Rodwell. Islam; Medieval (600 – 1500); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (J. M. Rodwell). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/2800
- "WHAT thinkest thou of him who treateth our RELIGION as a lie? He it is who trusteth away the orphan, And stirreth not others up to feed the poor." — Qur'an, Qur'an 107:1–3 (Sura Al-Ma'un, 'Religion'), tr. J. M. Rodwell; capitals as printed. Islam; Medieval (600 – 1500); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (J. M. Rodwell). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/2800
- "Do the right, and thou shalt continue upon the earth. Make the weeper to cease his plaint. Fleece not the widow woman." — Kheti (attributed), Teaching for King Merykara, §XII, tr. E. A. Wallis Budge, in The Teaching of Amen-em-apt (1924). Ancient Egyptian wisdom literature; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (E. A. Wallis Budge, 1924). Read it at: https://archive.org/details/teachingofamenem0000eawa
- "Commit no robbery (i.e., filch not away land) by means of the cubit of the fields When thou art assessing the bounds of the estate of the widow." — Amenemope, Instruction of Amenemope, ch. 6, tr. E. A. Wallis Budge, The Teaching of Amen-em-apt (1924); Budge's gloss in brackets kept as printed. Ancient Egyptian wisdom literature; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (E. A. Wallis Budge, 1924). Read it at: https://archive.org/details/teachingofamenem0000eawa
- "That the strong might not injure the weak, in order to protect the widows and orphans" — Hammurabi, Code of Hammurabi, epilogue, tr. L. W. King; opening of a longer sentence (the king set up his laws in Babylon for this purpose). Ancient Mesopotamia (Babylonian law); Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (L. W. King). Read it at: https://avalon.law.yale.edu/ancient/hamcode.asp
- "There were the old and wifeless, or widowers, the old and husbandless, or widows; the old and childless, or solitaries; and the young and fatherless, or orphans:—these four classes are the most destitute under heaven, and have none to whom they can tell [their wants], and king Wan, in the institution of his government with its benevolent action, made them the first objects of his regard." — Mencius, Mencius I.ii.5 (1B.5), tr. James Legge, The Life and Works of Mencius (1875), p. 148; Legge's brackets kept. Confucianism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Legge). Read it at: https://archive.org/details/lifeworksofmenci00mencuoft

## Everything passes; hold things lightly.

https://42maxims.com/maxims/everything-passes/ · Moral Rank 71.9 · 6 traditions · The 42

Nothing we see stays the same, not our troubles, our triumphs or the world around us. Remembering this can steady us in hard times and keep us gentle in good ones.

- "`All created things perish,' he who knows and sees this becomes passive in pain; this is the way to purity." — The Buddha, Dhammapada 277, tr. F. Max Müller. Buddhism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Müller). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/2017
- "Time is like a river made up of the events which happen, and a violent stream; for as soon as a thing has been seen, it is carried away, and another comes in its place, and this will be carried away too." — Marcus Aurelius, Meditations, Book IV.43, tr. George Long. Stoicism; Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (George Long). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/15877
- "Heracleitus is supposed to say that all things are in motion and nothing at rest; he compares them to the stream of a river, and says that you cannot go into the same water twice." — Heraclitus (as reported by Socrates in Plato), Plato, Cratylus 402a, tr. Benjamin Jowett. Greek philosophy; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Jowett). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/1616
- "One generation passeth away, and another generation cometh: but the earth abideth for ever." — Qoheleth (the Preacher), Ecclesiastes 1:4 (KJV). Judaism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "Be in this world as if you were a stranger or a traveler." — The Prophet Muhammad (narrated by Ibn 'Umar), Sahih al-Bukhari 6416. Islam; Medieval (600 – 1500); relation: similar; verified. Translation: Muhsin Khan translation, as given on sunnah.com. Read it at: https://sunnah.com/bukhari:6416
- "There is now a change again, and she is dead. The relation between these things is like the procession of the four seasons from spring to autumn, from winter to summer." — Zhuangzi, Zhuangzi, Book XVIII (Perfect Enjoyment), 2, on the death of his wife, tr. James Legge (Sacred Books of the East 40, 1891). Taoism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (James Legge). Read it at: https://archive.sacred-texts.com/tao/sbe40/sbe4002.htm

## Let your actions match your words.

https://42maxims.com/maxims/actions-over-words/ · Moral Rank 70.6 · 5 traditions · The 42

Fine words cost little; what we do shows what we really believe. Living out what we say, quietly and first, is how trust is built, in others and in ourselves.

- "He acts before he speaks, and afterwards speaks according to his actions." — Confucius, Analects 2.13 (Wei Zheng), tr. James Legge. Confucianism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Legge). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/4094
- "Like a beautiful flower, full of colour, but without scent, are the fine but fruitless words of him who does not act accordingly." — The Buddha (Dhammapada), Dhammapada, verse 51, tr. F. Max Müller. Buddhism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Max Müller). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/2017
- "But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves." — James, James 1:22 (KJV). Christianity; Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=James+1%3A22&version=KJV
- "Believers! why profess ye that which ye practise not? Most hateful is it to God that ye say that which ye do not." — The Qur'an, Qur'an 61:2–3 (Sura As-Saff, 'Battle Array'), tr. J. M. Rodwell. Islam; Medieval (600 – 1500); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (J. M. Rodwell). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/2800
- "Wherefore by their fruits ye shall know them." — Jesus, Matthew 7:20 (KJV). Christianity; Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "A learned man without works is a bee without honey" — Saadi, Gulistan, ch. VIII, maxim LXXXVI, tr. James Ross (1823), in Persian Literature, vol. 2 (Colonial Press, 1900). Persian poetry & literature; Medieval (600 – 1500); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (James Ross). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/13060

## Honour your father and your mother.

https://42maxims.com/maxims/honour-your-parents/ · Moral Rank 69.9 · 5 traditions · The 42

The people who raised us gave us our first world, however imperfectly. Many traditions ask us to meet them with care and respect, not just duty, and to let that gratitude show in how we treat them as they grow older.

- "Honour thy father and thy mother: that thy days may be long upon the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee." — Torah (Ten Commandments), Exodus 20:12 (KJV). Judaism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Exodus+20%3A12&version=KJV
- "The filial piety of now-a-days means the support of one's parents. But dogs and horses likewise are able to do something in the way of support;-- without reverence, what is there to distinguish the one support given from the other?" — Confucius, Analects 2.7 (Wei Zheng), tr. James Legge. Confucianism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Legge). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/4094
- "Thy Lord hath ordained that ye worship none but him; and, kindness to your parents, whether one or both of them attain to old age with thee: and say not to them, "Fie!" neither reproach them; but speak to them both with respectful speech;" — The Qur'an, Qur'an 17:23 (Sura Al-Isra, 'The Night Journey'), tr. J. M. Rodwell. Islam; Medieval (600 – 1500); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (J. M. Rodwell). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/2800
- "Let thy mother be to thee like unto a god! Let thy father be to thee like unto a god!" — Taittiriya Upanishad, Taittiriya Upanishad I.11.2, tr. F. Max Müller (Sacred Books of the East 15, 1884). Hinduism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (F. Max Müller). Read it at: https://archive.sacred-texts.com/hin/sbe15/sbe15032.htm
- "Let thy teacher be to thee like unto a god!" — Taittiriya Upanishad, Taittiriya Upanishad I.11.2, tr. F. Max Müller (Sacred Books of the East 15, 1884); the same charge honours mother, father and guest. Hinduism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (F. Max Müller). Read it at: https://archive.sacred-texts.com/hin/sbe15/sbe15032.htm
- "Thou shalt rise up before the hoary head, and honour the face of the old man, and fear thy God: I am the LORD." — Authors of the Torah, Leviticus 19:32 (KJV). Judaism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "When there are no elders the town is ruined, / And when the master dies the house is desolate." — Yoruba proverb, Yoruba aphorism 9 (couplet sayings), as recorded and translated by A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-Speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (1894), ch. XIII; line breaks shown as /. The saying is older than its 1894 recording.. Yoruba tradition; Modern (1800 – 1950); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (A. B. Ellis). Read it at: https://archive.sacred-texts.com/afr/yor/yor11.htm

## Be humble; pride goes before a fall.

https://42maxims.com/maxims/humility/ · Moral Rank 66.9 · 5 traditions · The 42

Those who lift themselves up tend to be brought low, while those who hold themselves lightly are trusted and remembered. Humility is not thinking less of ourselves, but seeing ourselves truly.

- "Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall." — Book of Proverbs, Proverbs 16:18 (KJV). Judaism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "And whosoever shall exalt himself shall be abased; and he that shall humble himself shall be exalted." — Jesus, Matthew 23:12 (KJV). Christianity; Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "He is free from self-display, and therefore he shines; from self-assertion, and therefore he is distinguished; from self-boasting, and therefore his merit is acknowledged;" — Laozi, Tao Te Ching, ch. 22, tr. James Legge. Taoism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Legge). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/216
- "Ego is the enemy." — Ryan Holiday, Ego Is the Enemy (Portfolio/Penguin, 2016) (book title; the phrase also recurs in the text); checked in the Internet Archive scan of that edition. Modern psychology & self-help; Contemporary (1950 – today); relation: similar; verified. Read it at: https://archive.org/details/egoisenemy0000holi
- "Be not proud because thou art learned; but discourse with the ignorant man, as with the sage. For no limit can be set to skill, neither is there any craftsman that possesseth full advantages." — Ptahhotep, The Instruction of Ptah-hotep, §1, tr. Battiscombe G. Gunn (1906). Ancient Egyptian wisdom literature; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Battiscombe G. Gunn). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/30508

## Leave things better than you found them.

https://42maxims.com/maxims/leave-it-better/ · Moral Rank 66.9 · 7 traditions · The 42

A simple measure for a day, a campsite or a life: did the world come out a little ahead for your having passed through?

- "Leave this world a little better than you found it." — Robert Baden-Powell, Last message to Scouts (published 1941); checked via Wikiquote, not the original. The sentence as printed begins "Try and leave this world…" (e.g. The Children's Newspaper, 8 March 1941, and Blassingame, Baden-Powell: Chief Scout of the World, 1966, both seen via Internet Archive full-text search); original manuscript not checked. Scouting movement; Modern (1800 – 1950); relation: expresses; probable. Read it at: https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Robert_Baden-Powell
- "Set your house in perfect order before you criticize the world." — Jordan B. Peterson, 12 Rules for Life (2018), Rule 6 (rule title); Random House Canada edition, checked against the book's contents as shown on Google Books (that listing drops punctuation). Modern psychology & self-help; Contemporary (1950 – today); relation: partial; verified. Read it at: https://books.google.com/books/about/12_Rules_for_Life.html?id=sxVHDwAAQBAJ
- "That man himself found a world full of carob trees. Just as my ancestors planted for me, I too am planting for my descendants." — Anonymous (the carob planter, told of Honi HaMe'aggel), Babylonian Talmud, Taanit 23a, William Davidson Edition (Koren-Steinsaltz). Judaism; Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: William Davidson Edition English translation, CC BY-NC (via Sefaria). Read it at: https://www.sefaria.org/Taanit.23a
- "And the LORD God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it." — Authors of the Torah, Genesis 2:15 (KJV); the first human is set in the garden to tend and keep it. Judaism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "It is the place where one of the faithful sows most corn, grass, and fruit, O Spitama Zarathushtra! where he waters ground that is dry, or drains ground that is too wet." — Avesta (Vendidad), Avesta, Vendidad, Fargard 3.4, tr. James Darmesteter (Sacred Books of the East 4, 1880); Ahura Mazda's answer to 'Which is the third place where the Earth feels most happy?'; footnote number removed. Zoroastrianism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (James Darmesteter). Read it at: https://www.avesta.org/vendidad/vd3sbe.htm
- "There is none amongst the Muslims who plants a tree or sows seeds, and then a bird, or a person or an animal eats from it, but is regarded as a charitable gift for him." — The Prophet Muhammad (narrated by Anas bin Malik), Sahih al-Bukhari 2320. Islam; Medieval (600 – 1500); relation: similar; verified. Translation: Muhsin Khan translation, as given on sunnah.com. Read it at: https://sunnah.com/bukhari:2320
- "Planters of parks or groves, those who build a bridge, a drinking place and well, and those who give monastic quarters. Their merit always grows by day and by night." — The Buddha, Vanaropa Sutta (SN 1.47), tr. Bhikkhu Sujato; verse line breaks shown as spaces. Buddhism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: Bhikkhu Sujato (CC0, SuttaCentral). Read it at: https://suttacentral.net/sn1.47/en/sujato
- "Look and listen for the welfare of the whole people and have always in view not only the present but also the coming generations, even those whose faces are yet beneath the surface of the ground—the unborn of the future Nation." — The Great Law of Peace (Haudenosaunee), The Constitution of the Five Nations, ed. Arthur C. Parker (1916), §28, pp. 38–39 (from the Seth Newhouse version); words addressed to a newly installed Confederate Lord; partial because it concerns leaders weighing future generations. Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) tradition; Modern (1800 – 1950); relation: partial; verified. Translation: English text as published by Parker (1916, public domain). Read it at: https://archive.org/details/constitutionoffi00parkuoft

## You reap what you sow.

https://42maxims.com/maxims/you-reap-what-you-sow/ · Moral Rank 66.0 · 5 traditions · The 42

What we do does not simply vanish; it comes back to shape our own lives. Traditions across the world picture our deeds returning to us, as surely as a harvest follows the seed or a shadow follows its body.

- "Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap." — Paul the Apostle, Galatians 6:7 (KJV). Christianity; Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "He that soweth iniquity shall reap vanity: and the rod of his anger shall fail." — Book of Proverbs, Proverbs 22:8 (KJV). Judaism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "according as he acts and according as he behaves, so will he be:--a man of good acts will become good, a man of bad acts, bad. He becomes pure by pure deeds, bad by bad deeds." — Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, Brihadaranyaka Upanishad IV.4.5, tr. F. Max Müller (Sacred Books of the East 15, 1884). Hinduism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (F. Max Müller). Read it at: https://archive.sacred-texts.com/hin/sbe15/sbe15076.htm
- "Ashes fly back in the face of him who throws them." — Yoruba proverb, Yoruba proverb 81, as recorded and translated by A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-Speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (1894), ch. XIII; Ellis glosses it as our "Curses come home to roost". The saying is older than its 1894 recording.. Yoruba tradition; Modern (1800 – 1950); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (A. B. Ellis). Read it at: https://archive.sacred-texts.com/afr/yor/yor11.htm
- "There are no special doors for calamity and happiness (in men's lot); they come as men themselves call them. Their recompenses follow good and evil as the shadow follows the substance." — Treatise of the Most Exalted One on Action and Response, The Thai-Shang Tractate of Actions and Their Retributions (Taishang Ganying Pian), 1, tr. James Legge (Sacred Books of the East 40, 1891); Legge's margin heading and footnote marker omitted. Taoism; Medieval (600 – 1500); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (James Legge). Read it at: https://archive.sacred-texts.com/tao/sbe40/sbe4018.htm

## Be present: the here and now is where life happens.

https://42maxims.com/maxims/be-present/ · Moral Rank 64.6 · 5 traditions · The 42

The past has gone and the future has not arrived. The present moment is the only place we can actually live, act and enjoy.

- "This is the real secret of life — to be completely engaged with what you are doing in the here and now.
