And instead of calling it work, realize it is play." — Alan Watts, The Essential Alan Watts (Celestial Arts, Berkeley), reissue of The Essence of Alan Watts (1977); checked in the Internet Archive scan of that edition. The 1977 Millbrae edition reads "realize that it is play". Western interpreters of Zen & Taoism; Contemporary (1950 – today); relation: expresses; verified. Read it at: https://archive.org/details/essentialalanwat0000watt
- "Our life is short; we must endeavour to gain the present time with best discretion and justice." — Marcus Aurelius, Meditations, Book IV, tr. Meric Casaubon. Stoicism; Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Casaubon). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/2680
- "Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof." — Jesus, Matthew 6:34 (KJV). Christianity; Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Matthew+6%3A34&version=KJV
- "Yet just as there is no time but the present, and no one except the all-and-everything, there is never anything to be gained—though the zest of the game is to pretend that there is." — Alan Watts, The Book: On the Taboo Against Knowing Who You Are (Pantheon Books, 1966); checked in the Internet Archive scan of that edition. Western interpreters of Zen & Taoism; Contemporary (1950 – today); relation: similar; verified. Read it at: https://archive.org/details/bookontabooagain00watt
- "The present alone is true and actual; it is the only time which possesses full reality, and our existence lies in it exclusively." — Arthur Schopenhauer, Counsels and Maxims (from Parerga and Paralipomena, 1851), ch. II, §5, tr. T. Bailey Saunders. 19th-century German philosophy; Modern (1800 – 1950); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (T. Bailey Saunders). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10715
- "Past and future obviously have no reality of their own." — Eckhart Tolle, The Power of Now (1997), ch. 3, p. 36 per Wikiquote (chapter and page not checked); wording checked in the Internet Archive scan of the New World Library edition (1999). Modern psychology & self-help; Contemporary (1950 – today); relation: similar; verified. Read it at: https://archive.org/details/powerofnowguidet0000toll_u4z4

## Seek peace, and pursue it.

https://42maxims.com/maxims/be-a-peacemaker/ · Moral Rank 64.5 · 6 traditions · The 42

Peace rarely arrives by itself; it is something we go after, in quarrels at home as much as between nations. To be the one who lowers the temperature, and who takes the offered hand, is honoured in nearly every tradition.

- "Depart from evil, and do good; seek peace, and pursue it." — Psalms, Psalm 34:14 (KJV). Judaism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "be of the disciples of Aaron, loving peace and pursuing peace, loving mankind and drawing them close to the Torah." — Hillel the Elder, Mishnah, Pirkei Avot 1:12, tr. Joshua Kulp (Mishnah Yomit). Judaism; Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: Sefaria / Mishnah Yomit by Dr. Joshua Kulp (CC BY). Read it at: https://www.sefaria.org/Pirkei_Avot.1.12
- "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God." — Jesus, Matthew 5:9 (KJV). Christianity; Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "And if they lean to peace, lean thou also to it; and put thy trust in God: for He is the Hearing, the Knowing." — The Qur'an, Qur'an 8:61 (Sura Al-Anfal, 'The Spoils'), tr. J. M. Rodwell. Islam; Medieval (600 – 1500); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (J. M. Rodwell). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/2800
- "Victory breeds hatred, for the conquered is unhappy. He who has given up both victory and defeat, he, the contented, is happy." — The Buddha, Dhammapada 201, tr. F. Max Müller. Buddhism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Max Müller). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/2017
- "Calm and repose are what he prizes; victory (by force of arms) is to him undesirable." — Laozi, Tao Te Ching, ch. 31, tr. James Legge. Taoism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: partial; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Legge). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/216

## Craving is the root of suffering.

https://42maxims.com/maxims/desire-is-the-root-of-suffering/ · Moral Rank 64.4 · 5 traditions · The 42

Much of our pain comes not from what happens, but from our grasping for things to be otherwise. Loosen the grip and the weight lightens.

- "The noble truth of the origination of stress: the craving that makes for further becoming." — The Buddha, Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta (SN 56.11), tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu. Buddhism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: Thanissaro Bhikkhu (free distribution). Read it at: https://www.accesstoinsight.org/tipitaka/sn/sn56/sn56.011.than.html
- "From lust comes grief, from lust comes fear; he who is free from lust knows neither grief nor fear." — The Buddha, Dhammapada 215, tr. F. Max Müller. Buddhism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Müller). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/2017
- "For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows." — Paul the Apostle, 1 Timothy 6:10 (KJV). Christianity; Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=1+Timothy+6%3A10&version=KJV
- "Desire’s a contract you make to be unhappy until you get what you want." — Naval Ravikant, Naval podcast, “Desire Is a Contract You Make to Be Unhappy” (10 Feb 2020), episode transcript on nav.al. Modern psychology & self-help; Contemporary (1950 – today); relation: similar; verified. Read it at: https://nav.al/desire
- "If one Ponders on objects of the sense, there springs Attraction; from attraction grows desire, Desire flames to fierce passion, passion breeds Recklessness; then the memory--all betrayed-- Lets noble purpose go, and saps the mind, Till purpose, mind, and man are all undone." — Krishna, Bhagavad Gita, ch. 2 (The Song Celestial), tr. Edwin Arnold; verse line breaks removed, capitals as printed. Hinduism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Edwin Arnold). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/2388
- "beware of the quality of covetousness, which is a grievous inner (?) malady. Let it not chance that thou fall thereinto. It setteth at variance fathers-in-law and the kinsmen of the daughter-in-law; it sundereth the wife and the husband. It gathereth unto itself all evils; it is the girdle of all wickedness." — Ptahhotep, The Instruction of Ptah-hotep, §19, tr. Battiscombe G. Gunn (1906); the "(?)" is the translator's. Ancient Egyptian wisdom literature; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Battiscombe G. Gunn). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/30508
- "Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth." — Jesus, Luke 12:15 (KJV). Christianity; Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10

## Admit your mistakes and put them right.

https://42maxims.com/maxims/own-your-mistakes/ · Moral Rank 64.0 · 5 traditions · The 42

Everyone falls short; what matters is what we do next. Owning a fault, rather than hiding it, is the first step to mending it, and a mended fault can leave us brighter than before.

- "To have faults and not to reform them,-- this, indeed, should be pronounced having faults." — Confucius, Analects 15.29, tr. James Legge. Confucianism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Legge). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/4094

Judaism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "He whose evil deeds are covered by good deeds, brightens up this world, like the moon when freed from clouds." — The Buddha, Dhammapada 173, tr. F. Max Müller. Buddhism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Müller). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/2017
- "Don’t make excuses, don’t blame any other person or any other thing." — Jocko Willink, “Extreme Ownership”, TEDxUniversityofNevada (2017). Management & engineering; Contemporary (1950 – today); relation: similar; verified. Read it at: https://amara.org/api/videos/uIqTGaZOkeOg/languages/en/subtitles/?format=txt
- "Bring thyself to account each day ere thou art summoned to a reckoning; for death, unheralded, shall come upon thee and thou shalt be called to give account for thy deeds." — Bahá’u’lláh, The Hidden Words, Arabic no. 31, tr. Shoghi Effendi. Bahá’í Faith; Modern (1800 – 1950); relation: similar; verified. Translation: authorised translation (Shoghi Effendi). ## Keep your promises; let your yes mean yes.

https://42maxims.com/maxims/keep-your-word/ · Moral Rank 63.5 · 5 traditions · The 42

A promise is a small piece of the future we give to someone else. Keeping it, or not making it lightly, is how trust grows, and how our words come to carry weight.

- "Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay." — Qoheleth (the Preacher), Ecclesiastes 5:5 (KJV). Islam; Medieval (600 – 1500); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (J. M. Rodwell). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/2800

## Listen more than you speak.

https://42maxims.com/maxims/listen-first/ · Moral Rank 62.6 · 4 traditions · The 42

Real listening is a kind of generosity, and a kind of humility too. When we assume the other person may know something we don't, conversations stop being contests and start teaching us.

- "This is the reason why we have two ears and only one mouth, that we may hear more and speak less." — Zeno of Citium, As reported by Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers VII (Life of Zeno), tr. C. D. Yonge. Stoicism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (C. D. Yonge). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/57342
- "Assume that the person you are listening to might know something you don't." — Jordan B. Peterson, 12 Rules for Life (2018), Rule 9 (rule title); Random House Canada edition, checked against the book's contents as shown on Google Books (that listing drops punctuation). Modern psychology & self-help; Contemporary (1950 – today); relation: similar; verified. Read it at: https://books.google.com/books/about/12_Rules_for_Life.html?id=sxVHDwAAQBAJ
- "He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him." — Book of Proverbs, Proverbs 18:13 (KJV). Judaism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "Seek first to understand, then to be understood." — Stephen R. Covey, The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People (1989), Habit 5 (habit title); checked on the FranklinCovey site. Modern psychology & self-help; Contemporary (1950 – today); relation: similar; verified. Read it at: https://www.franklincovey.com/habit-5/
- "let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath:" — James, James 1:19 (KJV). Christianity; Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10

## First, do no harm.

https://42maxims.com/maxims/do-no-harm/ · Moral Rank 61.6 · 4 traditions · The 42

Before we try to help, we can at least refuse to hurt. This simple restraint, shared by healers, monks and moralists, asks us to remember that every living being, like us, fears pain and loves life.

- "have two special objects in view with regard to diseases, namely, to do good or to do no harm." — Hippocrates, Epidemics, Book I, section 2, tr. Francis Adams (The Genuine Works of Hippocrates, 1849). Hippocratic medicine; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Francis Adams). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/72583
- "all breathing, existing, living, sentient creatures should not be slain, nor treated with violence, nor abused, nor tormented, nor driven away." — Mahavira (the Arhats), Acaranga Sutra, Book I, Lecture 4, Lesson 1, tr. Hermann Jacobi (Sacred Books of the East 22). Jainism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Hermann Jacobi). Read it at: https://archive.sacred-texts.com/jai/sbe22/sbe2220.htm
- "All men tremble at punishment, all men fear death; remember that you are like unto them, and do not kill, nor cause slaughter." — The Buddha, Dhammapada 129, tr. F. Max Müller. Buddhism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Max Müller). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/2017
- "Love worketh no ill to his neighbour: therefore love is the fulfilling of the law." — Paul the Apostle, Romans 13:10 (KJV). Christianity; Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10

## Choose your companions wisely.

https://42maxims.com/maxims/choose-your-friends/ · Moral Rank 60.4 · 4 traditions · The 42

We slowly become like the people we spend our days with. Seeking out good, honest friends is one of the surest ways to grow into a better person.

- "He that walketh with wise men shall be wise: but a companion of fools shall be destroyed." — Book of Proverbs, Proverbs 13:20 (KJV). Judaism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "Do not have evil-doers for friends, do not have low people for friends: have virtuous people for friends, have for friends the best of men." — The Buddha, Dhammapada 78, tr. F. Max Müller. Buddhism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Müller). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/2017
- "There are three friendships which are advantageous, and three which are injurious. Friendship with the upright; friendship with the sincere; and friendship with the man of much observation:-- these are advantageous." — Confucius, Analects 16.4, tr. James Legge. Confucianism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Legge). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/4094
- "A man follows the religion of his friend; so each one should consider whom he makes his friend." — The Prophet Muhammad (narrated by Abu Hurayrah), Sunan Abi Dawud 4833. Islam; Medieval (600 – 1500); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: Ahmad Hasan translation, as given on sunnah.com. Read it at: https://sunnah.com/abudawud:4833

## Keep learning, all your life.

https://42maxims.com/maxims/keep-learning/ · Moral Rank 60.3 · 4 traditions · The 42

Learning is not a stage we finish but a way of staying awake to the world. Traditions far apart describe it as a quiet pleasure, the mark of someone wise enough to know there is always more to hear.

- "Is it not pleasant to learn with a constant perseverance and application?" — Confucius, Analects 1.1 (Xue Er), tr. James Legge. Confucianism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Legge). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/4094

- "Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom: and with all thy getting get understanding." — Book of Proverbs, Proverbs 4:7 (KJV). Judaism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "Learning without thought is labour lost; thought without learning is perilous." — Confucius, Analects 2.15, tr. James Legge. Confucianism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Legge). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/4094
- "Seeking knowledge is a duty upon every Muslim," — The Prophet Muhammad (narrated by Anas bin Malik), Sunan Ibn Majah 224; sunnah.com notes this opening phrase is authentic through many routes, the rest of the narration is weak and is not quoted. Islam; Medieval (600 – 1500); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: English translation as given on sunnah.com. Read it at: https://sunnah.com/ibnmajah:224
- "In sandy soil, when deep you delve, you reach the springs below; / The more you learn, the freer streams of wisdom flow." — Tiruvalluvar, Tirukkural, kural 396, tr. G. U. Pope (1886); verse line break shown as /. Tamil ethics (Tirukkural); Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (G. U. Pope, W. H. Drew, J. Lazarus, F. W. Ellis). Read it at: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Tirukural/Chapter_40

## Be patient; endure, and let things ripen.

https://42maxims.com/maxims/patience/ · Moral Rank 60.3 · 5 traditions · The 42

Much of what matters grows slowly and cannot be hurried. Patience is the quiet strength that holds steady through difficulty and waits for the right moment.

## Find meaning in the struggle itself.

https://42maxims.com/maxims/embrace-the-struggle/ · Moral Rank 59.3 · 5 traditions · The 42

Sisyphus pushes his boulder up the hill forever. The ancient myth was a punishment; the modern reading asks whether the effort itself can be enough.

- "One must imagine Sisyphus happy." — Albert Camus, The Myth of Sisyphus (1942), title essay, closing sentence; tr. - "we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience; And patience, experience; and experience, hope:" — Paul the Apostle, Romans 5:3-4 (KJV). Christianity; Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "A hero ventures forth from the world of common day into a region of supernatural wonder: fabulous forces are there encountered and a decisive victory is won: the hero comes back from this mysterious adventure with the power to bestow boons on his fellow man." — Joseph Campbell, The Hero with a Thousand Faces (1949), introduction; p. 30 in the 1968 Princeton edition; checked in the Internet Archive scan of the 1949 Princeton first edition, which reads "fellow man" (the Joseph Campbell Foundation site has "fellow men"). Comparative mythology; Modern (1800 – 1950); relation: partial; verified. Read it at: https://archive.org/details/herowiththousand0000unse

## When you fall, get back up.

https://42maxims.com/maxims/get-back-up/ · Moral Rank 57.6 · 4 traditions · The 42

Falling is not the failure; staying down is. Traditions far apart in time and place honour the person who stumbles, gathers themselves, and rises again, as many times as it takes.

- "For a just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again: but the wicked shall fall into mischief." — Book of Proverbs, Proverbs 24:16 (KJV). Judaism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "Our greatest glory is, not in never falling; but in rising every time we fall." — Oliver Goldsmith (often misattributed to Confucius), The Citizen of the World (1762), vol. 1, Letter VII. Spoken by Goldsmith's fictional Chinese narrator, who credits Confucius; the line is not found in Confucius's works (see Quote Investigator, https://quoteinvestigator.com/2014/05/27/rising/). Spelling modernised from the long s.. English poetry & literature; Early modern (1500 – 1800); relation: expresses; verified. Read it at: https://archive.org/details/bim_eighteenth-century_the-citizen-of-the-world_goldsmith-oliver_1762_1_0
- "From the military school of life.—That which does not kill me, makes me stronger." — Friedrich Nietzsche, Twilight of the Idols (1889), “Maxims and Missiles” 8, tr. Anthony M. Ludovici. 19th-century German philosophy; Modern (1800 – 1950); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Anthony M. Ludovici). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/52263
- "If one is carrying water, and it gets spilt, so long as the calabash is not broken one can still get more." — Yoruba proverb, Yoruba proverb 146, as recorded and translated by A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-Speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (1894), ch. XIII. The saying is older than its 1894 recording.. Yoruba tradition; Modern (1800 – 1950); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (A. B. Ellis). Read it at: https://archive.sacred-texts.com/afr/yor/yor11.htm

## Pursue what is meaningful, not what is merely profitable.

https://42maxims.com/maxims/pursue-meaning/ · Moral Rank 57.2 · 4 traditions · The 42

Chase the thing that matters to you rather than the quick reward. A life built around meaning tends to carry its own momentum.

- "Pursue what is meaningful (not what is expedient)." — Jordan B. Peterson, 12 Rules for Life (2018), Rule 7 (rule title); Random House Canada edition, checked against the book's contents as shown on Google Books (that listing drops punctuation). Modern psychology & self-help; Contemporary (1950 – today); relation: expresses; verified. Read it at: https://books.google.com/books/about/12_Rules_for_Life.html?id=sxVHDwAAQBAJ
- "Do what you love and the money will follow; if you say that getting the money is the most important thing, you will spend your life completely wasting your time." — Alan Watts (popular attribution), Popular paraphrase of the 'What if money was no object?' talk; exact wording not traced. The second clause is widely quoted from the talk in books (seen via Internet Archive full-text search) but no transcript or recording was checked; "Do what you love, the money will follow" is not his phrase (it is the title of a 1987 book by Marsha Sinetar). Western interpreters of Zen & Taoism; Contemporary (1950 – today); relation: similar; unverified. No source yet.
- "For what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?" — Jesus, Matthew 16:26 (KJV). Christianity; Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "If a man knows the wherefore of his existence, then the manner of it can take care of itself." — Friedrich Nietzsche, Twilight of the Idols (1889), “Maxims and Missiles” 12, tr. Anthony M. Ludovici (often quoted as “He who has a why to live can bear almost any how”). 19th-century German philosophy; Modern (1800 – 1950); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Anthony M. Ludovici). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/52263
- "Follow your bliss and don't be afraid, and doors will open where you didn't know they were going to be." — Joseph Campbell, The Power of Myth (1988, with Bill Moyers), p. 120; checked on the Joseph Campbell Foundation site. Comparative mythology; Contemporary (1950 – today); relation: similar; verified. Read it at: https://www.jcf.org/post/doors-will-open

## Do your work wholeheartedly and with skill.

https://42maxims.com/maxims/mastery/ · Moral Rank 56.6 · 5 traditions · The 42

Whatever is in front of you, give it your full strength. Skill grows quietly out of repeated, careful effort, and in time it opens doors.

- "Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might; for there is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in the grave, whither thou goest." — Qoheleth (the Preacher), Ecclesiastes 9:10 (KJV). Judaism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Ecclesiastes+9%3A10&version=KJV
- "Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings; he shall not stand before mean men." — Book of Proverbs, Proverbs 22:29 (KJV). Judaism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Proverbs+22%3A29&version=KJV
- "We are what we repeatedly do. Excellence, then, is not an act, but a habit." — Will Durant (often misattributed to Aristotle), The Story of Philosophy (1926), summarising Aristotle; listed as misattributed on Wikiquote. Popular philosophy; Modern (1800 – 1950); relation: similar; misattributed. Read it at: https://en.wikiquote.org/wiki/Aristotle
- "And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men;" — Paul the Apostle, Colossians 3:23 (KJV). Christianity; Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "Let right deeds be Thy motive, not the fruit which comes from them. And live in action! Labour!" — Krishna (Bhagavad Gita), Bhagavad Gita, ch. 2 (The Song Celestial), tr. Edwin Arnold. Hinduism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Edwin Arnold). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/2388
- "But all things excellent are as difficult as they are rare." — Baruch Spinoza, Ethics (1677), Part V, Prop. XLII, Note (the closing words of the book), tr. R. H. M. Elwes. Rationalism; Early modern (1500 – 1800); relation: partial; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (R. H. M. Elwes). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/3800

## Great things begin with small steps.

https://42maxims.com/maxims/small-beginnings/ · Moral Rank 56.1 · 4 traditions · The 42

Every large work starts as something tiny and easy to overlook. Taking the next small step, and being faithful in little things, is how anything worthwhile gets built.

- "The tree which fills the arms grew from the tiniest sprout; the tower of nine storeys rose from a (small) heap of earth; the journey of a thousand li commenced with a single step." — Laozi, Tao Te Ching, ch. 64, tr. James Legge. Taoism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Legge). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/216
- "For who hath despised the day of small things?" — Book of Zechariah, Zechariah 4:10 (KJV). Judaism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much:" — Jesus, Luke 16:10 (KJV). Christianity; Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "Continual sweepings make a dust-heap." — Yoruba proverb, Yoruba proverb 6, as recorded and translated by A. B. Ellis, The Yoruba-Speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast of West Africa (1894), ch. XIII. The saying is older than its 1894 recording.. Yoruba tradition; Modern (1800 – 1950); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (A. B. Ellis). Read it at: https://archive.sacred-texts.com/afr/yor/yor11.htm

## Do what is just, even when it costs you.

https://42maxims.com/maxims/justice/ · Moral Rank 55.9 · 4 traditions · The 42

Justice asks us to be fair when fairness is inconvenient: to our rivals, to strangers, and against our own interest. Many traditions hold that it is better to suffer a wrong than to do one, and that a fair heart is worth more than any advantage.

- "That which is altogether just shalt thou follow, that thou mayest live, and inherit the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee." — Hebrew Bible (Torah), Deuteronomy 16:20 (KJV). Judaism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?" — Book of Micah, Micah 6:8 (KJV). Judaism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "O ye who believe! stand fast to justice, when ye bear witness before God, though it be against yourselves, or your parents, or your kindred, whether the party be rich or poor." — The Qur'an, Qur'an 4:135 (Sura An-Nisa, 'Women'), tr. J. M. Rodwell. Islam; Medieval (600 – 1500); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (J. M. Rodwell). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/2800
- "I should not like either, but if I must choose between them, I would rather suffer than do." — Socrates (in Plato), Plato, Gorgias 469c, tr. Benjamin Jowett; Socrates on whether he would rather suffer or do injustice. Greek philosophy; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Jowett). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/1672
- "He who acts unjustly acts impiously." — Marcus Aurelius, Meditations, Book IX.1, tr. George Long. Stoicism; Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (George Long). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/15877

## There is a time for everything; give your days a rhythm.

https://42maxims.com/maxims/a-time-for-everything/ · Moral Rank 51.9 · 3 traditions · The 42

Life moves in seasons and cycles. A steady rhythm of rising, working, eating and resting makes room for everything else.

- "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven." — Qoheleth (the Preacher), Ecclesiastes 3:1 (KJV). Judaism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Buddhism; Contemporary (1950 – today); relation: partial; unverified. No source yet.
- "Nothing for me is too early nor too late, which is in due time for thee. Everything is fruit to me which thy seasons bring, O Nature:" — Marcus Aurelius, Meditations IV.23, tr. George Long. ## Seek the middle way; avoid extremes.

https://42maxims.com/maxims/moderation/ · Moral Rank 49.1 · 4 traditions · The 42

Too much and too little both lead us astray. Again and again the old teachers point to a balanced path between the extremes, harder to find than either, but steadier to walk.

- "Virtue then is in a sense a mean state, since it certainly has an aptitude for aiming at the mean." — Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book II, ch. 6, tr. D. P. Chase. Greek philosophy; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Chase). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/8438
- "Perfect is the virtue which is according to the Constant Mean! Rare for a long time has been its practise among the people." — Confucius, Analects 6.27 (Yong Ye), tr. James Legge. Confucianism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Legge). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/4094
- "Avoiding both of these extremes, the middle way realized by the Tathagata — producing vision, producing knowledge — leads to calm, to direct knowledge, to self-awakening, to Unbinding." — The Buddha, Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta (SN 56.11), tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu. Buddhism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: Thanissaro Bhikkhu (free distribution). Read it at: https://www.accesstoinsight.org/tipitaka/sn/sn56/sn56.011.than.html
- "Be not righteous over much; neither make thyself over wise: why shouldest thou destroy thyself?" — Qoheleth (the Preacher), Ecclesiastes 7:16 (KJV). Judaism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: partial; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10

## Be kind to animals.

https://42maxims.com/maxims/be-kind-to-animals/ · Moral Rank 48.7 · 4 traditions · The 42

Animals feel hunger, fear and pain, and many of them live in our care or at our mercy. Traditions far apart treat the way we treat them as a quiet measure of our character, and kindness to a thirsty creature as a good deed in its own right.

- "A righteous man regardeth the life of his beast: but the tender mercies of the wicked are cruel." — Book of Proverbs, Proverbs 12:10 (KJV). Judaism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "A man is not an elect (Ariya) because he injures living creatures; because he has pity on all living creatures, therefore is a man called Ariya." — The Buddha, Dhammapada 270, tr. F. Max Müller. Buddhism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Müller). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/2017
- ""Is there a reward for us in serving (the) animals?" He replied, "Yes, there is a reward for serving any animate."" — The Prophet Muhammad, Sahih al-Bukhari 2363 (narrated by Abu Huraira), the Prophet's answer after telling of a man forgiven for giving water to a thirsty dog. Islam; Medieval (600 – 1500); relation: similar; verified. Translation: Muhsin Khan translation, as given on sunnah.com. Read it at: https://sunnah.com/bukhari:2363
- "Knowing them, a wise man should not act sinfully towards animals, nor cause others to act so, nor allow others to act so." — Mahavira, Acaranga Sutra, Book I, Lecture 1, Lesson 6, tr. Hermann Jacobi (Sacred Books of the East 22). Jainism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Hermann Jacobi). Read it at: https://archive.sacred-texts.com/jai/sbe22/sbe2208.htm

## Your thoughts shape your life.

https://42maxims.com/maxims/thoughts-shape-life/ · Moral Rank 48.2 · 5 traditions · Emerging

What we dwell on becomes the lens we see through, and then the ground we stand on. Tending the mind is tending the life.

- "All that we are is the result of what we have thought: it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts." — The Buddha, Dhammapada 1, tr. F. Max Müller. Buddhism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Müller). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/2017

Read it at: https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Romans+12%3A2&version=KJV
- "I think, therefore I am (COGITO ERGO SUM)." — René Descartes, Discourse on Method (1637), Part IV, tr. John Veitch. Rationalism; Early modern (1500 – 1800); relation: partial; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Veitch). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/59
- "Everything can be taken from a man but one thing: the last of the human freedoms—to choose one's attitude in any given set of circumstances, to choose one's own way." — Viktor E. Frankl, Man's Search for Meaning (1946; English tr. 1959), tr. Ilse Lasch; checked in an Internet Archive scan of the English edition (punctuation corrected to match it). Modern psychology & self-help; Modern (1800 – 1950); relation: partial; verified. Read it at: https://archive.org/details/manssearchformea0000vikt_p2n1
- "And here they say that a person consists of desires. And as is his desire, so is his will; and as is his will, so is his deed; and whatever deed he does, that he will reap." — Brihadaranyaka Upanishad (Yajnavalkya), Brihadaranyaka Upanishad IV.4.5, tr. ## Happiness is reality minus expectations.

https://42maxims.com/maxims/happiness-and-expectations/ · Moral Rank 44.2 · 5 traditions · Emerging

A popular modern formula. When expectations outrun reality, disappointment fills the gap; holding them lightly leaves room for contentment.

- "Happiness equals reality minus expectations." — Anonymous / popular saying, Origin not established; widely circulated online. Popular / anonymous sayings; Contemporary (1950 – today); relation: expresses; unverified. No source yet.
- "My third maxim was to endeavor always to conquer myself rather than fortune, and change my desires rather than the order of the world." — René Descartes, Discourse on Method (1637), Part III, tr. John Veitch. Rationalism; Early modern (1500 – 1800); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Veitch). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/59
- "Demand not that events should happen as you wish; but wish them to happen as they do happen, and you will go on well." — Epictetus, Enchiridion VIII, tr. Thomas Wentworth Higginson. Stoicism; Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Higginson). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/45109
- "for I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content." — Paul the Apostle, Philippians 4:11 (KJV). Christianity; Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "He who is satisfied with his lot is rich;" — Laozi, Tao Te Ching, ch. 33, tr. James Legge. Taoism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: partial; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Legge). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/216
- "The desire for more positive experience is itself a negative experience. And, paradoxically, the acceptance of one’s negative experience is itself a positive experience." — Mark Manson, The Subtle Art of Not Giving a F*ck (2016), ch. 1 “Don’t Try”, p. 9; checked via Wikiquote, not the book. ## Rise to your work.

https://42maxims.com/maxims/rise-to-your-work/ · Moral Rank 44.1 · 3 traditions · Emerging

On the mornings when we would rather stay in bed, the work in front of us is still ours to do. Many traditions treat idleness as a slow loss and honest effort as part of what it means to live fully.

- "In the morning when thou risest unwillingly, let this thought be present,--I am rising to the work of a human being." — Marcus Aurelius, Meditations, Book V.1, tr. George Long. Stoicism; Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (George Long). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/15877
- "He who does not rouse himself when it is time to rise, who, though young and strong, is full of sloth, whose will and thought are weak, that lazy and idle man will never find the way to knowledge." — The Buddha, Dhammapada 280, tr. F. Max Müller. Buddhism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Müller). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/2017
- "Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise:" — Book of Proverbs, Proverbs 6:6 (KJV). Judaism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10

## Give full measure: deal honestly in trade.

https://42maxims.com/maxims/deal-honestly-in-trade/ · Moral Rank 41.7 · 3 traditions · Emerging

Fair weights and honest measures are among the oldest moral rules we know. Cheating in small ways, a short measure here or a fake mixed in with the genuine there, wears away the trust that every exchange depends on.

- "A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight." — Book of Proverbs, Proverbs 11:1 (KJV). Judaism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10
- "And give full measure when you measure, and weigh with just balance." — The Qur'an, Qur'an 17:35 (Sura Al-Isra, 'The Night Journey'), tr. J. M. Rodwell. Islam; Medieval (600 – 1500); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (J. M. Rodwell). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/2800
- "if he uses a short cubit, a narrow measure, light weights, and a small pint; mixes spurious articles with the genuine; and (thus) amasses illicit gain;" — Treatise of the Most Exalted One on Action and Response, The Thai-Shang Tractate of Actions and Their Retributions (Taishang Ganying Pian), 4 (from its list of wrong deeds), tr. James Legge (Sacred Books of the East 40, 1891). Taoism; Medieval (600 – 1500); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (James Legge). Read it at: https://archive.sacred-texts.com/tao/sbe40/sbe4018.htm
- "Ye shall do no unrighteousness in judgment, in meteyard, in weight, or in measure. Just balances, just weights, a just ephah, and a just hin, shall ye have: I am the LORD your God, which brought you out of the land of Egypt." — Authors of the Torah, Leviticus 19:35–36 (KJV). Judaism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10

Talents are a starting point, not a verdict. The useful comparison is with your own past self, and every honest effort moves the line.

- "Compare yourself to who you were yesterday, not to who someone else is today." — Jordan B. Read it at: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mindset_(book)

## Know yourself.

https://42maxims.com/maxims/know-yourself/ · Moral Rank 41.4 · 3 traditions · Emerging

Understanding the world begins close to home. To look honestly at our own motives, limits and ignorance is a lifelong task, and perhaps the beginning of every other kind of wisdom.

- "the unexamined life is not worth living" — Socrates (in Plato), Plato, Apology 38a, tr. Benjamin Jowett. Greek philosophy; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Jowett). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/1656

Confucianism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: similar; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Legge). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/4094

https://42maxims.com/maxims/peter-principle/ · Moral Rank 38.5 · 3 traditions · Emerging

Confucianism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: partial; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Legge). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/4094

Taoism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: partial; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (James Legge). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/216

## Life contains suffering; begin by accepting it.

https://42maxims.com/maxims/life-is-suffering/ · Moral Rank 34.5 · 2 traditions · Emerging

## A few causes drive most results (the 80/20 rule).

https://42maxims.com/maxims/vital-few/ · Moral Rank 33.0 · 4 traditions · Emerging

Effort and outcome are rarely in proportion. Find the vital few things that matter and give them your best attention.

- "For many outcomes, roughly 80% of consequences come from 20% of causes." — Joseph M. Juran (after Vilfredo Pareto), Pareto principle, as summarised by Wikipedia (paraphrase, not a direct quote). Management & engineering; Modern (1800 – 1950); relation: expresses; probable. Read it at: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pareto_principle
- "We should forget about small efficiencies, say about 97% of the time: premature optimization is the root of all evil. Yet we should not pass up our opportunities in that critical 3%." — Donald Knuth, "Structured Programming with go to Statements", Computing Surveys 6:4 (December 1974), §1; wording checked against a scan of the paper (the paper prints "3 %"). Computer science; Contemporary (1950 – today); relation: similar; verified. Read it at: https://pic.plover.com/knuth-GOTO.pdf
- "Occupy thyself with few things, says the philosopher, if thou wouldst be tranquil." — Marcus Aurelius, Meditations IV.24, tr. George Long (kept as a related saying about focus; not used as independent attestation of the 80/20 rule). Stoicism; Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: partial; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (George Long). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/15877
- "Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things: But one thing is needful:" — Jesus, Luke 10:41-42 (KJV) (kept as a related saying about focus; not used as independent attestation of the 80/20 rule). Christianity; Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: partial; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Luke+10%3A41-42&version=KJV

## More choice does not always mean more happiness.

https://42maxims.com/maxims/paradox-of-choice/ · Moral Rank 32.4 · 3 traditions · Emerging

An endless menu can leave us anxious and second-guessing. Sometimes choosing 'good enough' and letting go is the wiser path.

- "Eliminating consumer choices can greatly reduce anxiety for shoppers." — Barry Schwartz, The Paradox of Choice (2004): summary via Wikipedia (paraphrase, not a direct quote). Modern psychology & self-help; Contemporary (1950 – today); relation: expresses; probable. Read it at: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Paradox_of_Choice
- "He whose (desires) are few gets them; he whose (desires) are many goes astray." — Laozi, Tao Te Ching, ch. 22, tr. James Legge. Taoism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: partial; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Legge). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/216
- "Better is the sight of the eyes than the wandering of the desire: this is also vanity and vexation of spirit." — Qoheleth (the Preacher), Ecclesiastes 6:9 (KJV). ## Advantage tends to compound: those who have, get more.

https://42maxims.com/maxims/matthew-effect/ · Moral Rank 26.4 · 2 traditions · Emerging

Early advantages (a head start, a good name, a little capital) tend to attract more of the same, while those with little often find even that slipping away. The Gospel of Matthew states the pattern twice, and in 1968 the sociologists Robert K. Merton and Harriet Zuckerman named it the Matthew effect. Seeing it clearly invites us to share a head start generously and to lift up those who begin behind.

- "For unto every one that hath shall be given, and he shall have abundance: but from him that hath not shall be taken away even that which he hath." — Jesus, Matthew 25:29 (KJV), closing the Parable of the Talents. Christianity; Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Matthew+25%3A29&version=KJV
- "For whosoever hath, to him shall be given, and he shall have more abundance: but whosoever hath not, from him shall be taken away even that he hath." — Jesus, Matthew 13:12 (KJV), explaining why Jesus teaches in parables. Christianity; Classical (200 BCE – 600 CE); relation: expresses; verified. Translation: King James Version (public domain). Read it at: https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Matthew+13%3A12&version=KJV
- "It is the Way of Heaven to diminish superabundance, and to supplement deficiency. It is not so with the way of man. He takes away from those who have not enough to add to his own superabundance." — Laozi, Tao Te Ching, ch. 77, tr. James Legge. A partial match: Laozi describes the way of man as taking from those who have little to add to those who have much, which is the pattern the Matthew effect names, and sets it against the Way of Heaven, which does the opposite.. Taoism; Ancient (before 200 BCE); relation: partial; verified. Translation: public-domain translation (Legge). Read it at: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/216
